chunk.text: 19 The bearings of passive contacts are plotted by a computer and this data can be used by tactical system operators to estimate the range, course and speed of the ship being detected. This process is called target motion analysis (TMA) and an estimated position, course and speed of the other vessel is referred to as a solution. The process of determining the range of a passive sonar contact can be significantly improved by the submarine altering course and/or speed as the subsequent change in bearing movement allows the command team to refine the solution, in particular the contact’s range. Changing the submarine’s course and/or speed to determine the range of passive contacts is called a ranging manoeuvre. The TMA process can also be refined using the additional acoustic evidence available. For instance, if a passive sonar contact has the acoustic characteristic of a large merchant vessel, the submarine’s command team can work to find solutions at speeds typical for such a vessel. Equally, if the sonar operators hear trawl noise, then the command team will classify the contact as a vessel engaged in fishing, and find TMA solutions at speeds typical for such a vessel. The workload of sonar and tactical system operators is a function of the number of contacts being detected and analysed. Figure 15 illustrates the passive TMA process prior to the collision. The submarine’s track, including the ranging manoeuvre, is shown in black and two possible TMA solutions are also shown. The more distant contact (shown in green) is a solution using a typical merchant vessel speed of 10kts, and the closer contact (shown in red) is a solution for a vessel speed of 2.8kts, representative of Karen’s actual relative movement. 1.8.3 Close quarters procedures In the event of a deep submarine making a sonar detection of a new contact that could present a risk to the submarine, the command team would undertake a close quarters procedure. This was a rapid, predetermined set of reactions intended to avoid collision. The Royal Navy has not disclosed to the MAIB the nature of the close quarters procedures in use by its submarines or the detail of the circumstances in which such action would be taken. 1.9 PASSAGE PLANNING 1.9.1 Royal Navy guidance The Admiralty Manual of Navigation Volume 1, The Principles of Navigation, Book of Reference (BR) 45(1) is the Royal Navy’s primary reference for the planning

extraction.source_assessment: Page 6 describes passive-sonar target motion analysis, classification-dependent solution assumptions, ranging manoeuvres, operator workload, and submarine close-quarters procedures. It illustrates alternative TMA solutions but does not find that a particular assumption, classification, workload condition, or procedure caused or contributed to the casualty. For example, the statement The workload of sonar and tactical system operators is a function of the number of contacts being detected and analysed. is methodological background, not a finding of excessive workload or impaired monitoring. The passage therefore contains no qualifying investigator finding, causal conclusion, or explicit safety issue from which to extract a lesson card. This rejection is based on the passage's evidential character, not its compatibility with the example runtime states.

chunk.report_title: MAIBInvReport 13/2020 - Stena Superfast VII and Royal Navy Submarine - Marine Incident
chunk.text: 20 SECTION 2 – ANALYSIS 2. 1 AIM The aim of the analysis is to determine the causes and circumstances of the near miss as a basis for making recommendations to prevent similar events occurring in the future. 2.2 SUMMARY During safety training in the North Channel, the command team of a submerged submarine did not take sufficient action to prevent the ferry, Stena Superfast VII, passing inside its go-deep range. This was an unsafe event and placed the ferry’s passengers and crew, as well as the submarine and its crew, in immediate danger. Rapid and effective action by Stena Superfast VII’s bridge team reduced the risk of collision. This section of the report will assess the causes and circumstances of the incident including safety-critical decision-making on board the submarine. The RN co-operated with the MAIB’s investigation to the maximum extent possible within the boundary of operational security. The submarine’s actual speed is unknown, but 6kts has been used as a basis for the calculations in this section. 2.3 THE NEAR MISS 2.3. 1 The submarine’s turn towards the ferry When the submarine’s control room team initially detected Stena Superfast VII visually, they estimated it to be at a range of 9000yds-10000yds. Appreciating that the ferry was heading almost straight towards the submarine, the OOW decided to alter course to open away from its projected track; this decision was taken when the range was estimated to be 6000yds. At a speed of 21kts, Stena Superfast VII would cover 6000yds in 8mins 34secs. This is an estimate of the time available for the submarine’s OOW to take avoiding action. However, the submarine’s OOW had estimated the ferry’s speed as 15kts, so would have incorrectly calculated that it would take the ferry 12mins to travel 6000yds. Therefore, the OOW almost certainly assessed that there was significantly more time to take avoiding action than was actually the case. Having made the decision to turn to port towards the ferry, the vessels were then converging, and the calculation can be refined using the combined speeds of 27kts, or just 6mins 40secs for the submarine and the ferry to close the 6000yds. This is a significantly lower estimate of the time available to take action to avoid the approaching ferry. Had the submarine been turned to starboard and away from the ferry, the resultant closing speed would be just 15kts, or an estimate of 12mins

extraction.source_assessment: The passage provides explicit causal analysis of underestimated contact speed and manoeuvre-dependent closing time, together with findings about insufficient avoidance and effective bridge-team action. Submarine-specific clearance doctrine and illustrative manoeuvres are not transferable prescriptions.

warning_signs: Available action time is based on an unverified contact-speed estimate.
A lower assumed contact speed produces a longer apparent time to encounter.
card.investigator_finding: The submarine OOW underestimated the ferry's speed and almost certainly assessed that substantially more time was available for avoidance than was actually available.
card.transferable_lesson: Check the speed assumptions underlying an available-time assessment; an underestimated approaching contact speed can create unjustified confidence that action can wait.
non_transfer_conditions: The passage does not establish that any future speed measurement is erroneous.
The accident's numerical speeds and times are not operational thresholds.

supporting_quotes.quote: However, the submarine’s OOW had estimated the ferry’s speed as 15kts, so would have incorrectly calculated that it would take the ferry 12mins to travel 6000yds.
Therefore, the OOW almost certainly assessed that there was significantly more time to take avoiding action than was actually the case.

lessons.potential_decision_use: Flag an avoidance-timing justification that depends on uncertain or contradicted contact speed for verification and uncertainty-aware reassessment.
required_live_evidence: An approaching contact and an available-time assessment derived from its estimated speed.
Explicit speed uncertainty or independent evidence contradicting the speed assumption before asserting underestimation.
prohibited_inferences: Do not infer speed error merely from a developing close encounter.
Do not infer range overestimation from this passage's initial range estimates.
Do not assign COLREG roles or infer sensing methods in a future encounter.

warning_signs: An avoidance proposal changes relative motion but retains the pre-manoeuvre time estimate.
A manoeuvre intended to open clearance instead produces convergence.
card.investigator_finding: The submarine's turn towards the ferry made the vessels converge, reducing the estimated time available when combined speeds were considered.
card.transferable_lesson: Evaluate avoidance proposals using the resulting relative motion, including own-ship movement, rather than relying on contact travel time or the intended purpose of the turn.
non_transfer_conditions: The passage's port/starboard comparison is specific to its geometry.
The submarine speed used in the analysis was an assumption, not a known measurement.

supporting_quotes.quote: Having made the decision to turn to port towards the ferry, the vessels were then converging, and the calculation can be refined using the combined speeds of 27kts, or just 6mins 40secs for the submarine and the ferry to close the 6000yds.
This is a significantly lower estimate of the time available to take action to avoid the approaching ferry.

lessons.potential_decision_use: Require a post-proposal relative-motion assessment and identify proposals that shorten the available response time despite an intention to open away.
required_live_evidence: Own-ship and contact motion sufficient to assess relative motion.
The proposed or executed manoeuvre and its predicted or observed effect on convergence and encounter timing.
prohibited_inferences: Do not prescribe either turn direction from the accident example.
Do not assume every turn towards a contact causes an unsafe encounter.
Do not treat simple range divided by closing speed as a substitute for a geometry-appropriate CPA/TCPA assessment.

warning_signs: Avoidance action remains insufficient to protect an applicable safety boundary.
card.investigator_finding: The submarine team's insufficient action allowed an unsafe intrusion inside its go-deep range, while rapid and effective action by the ferry bridge team reduced collision risk.
card.transferable_lesson: Assess whether avoidance action actually achieves the required separation; prompt, effective intervention can reduce risk when an encounter remains unsafe.
non_transfer_conditions: Go-deep range is submarine-specific and is not a surface-vessel clearance standard.
The passage does not identify the ferry's manoeuvre or establish a generally applicable action magnitude.

supporting_quotes.quote: During safety training in the North Channel, the command team of a submerged submarine did not take sufficient action to prevent the ferry, Stena Superfast VII, passing inside its go-deep range.
Rapid and effective action by Stena Superfast VII’s bridge team reduced the risk of collision.

lessons.potential_decision_use: Challenge passive continuation or nominal avoidance when live evidence shows that the applicable separation requirement remains unmet.
required_live_evidence: A live collision-risk assessment or predicted breach of an independently applicable separation limit.
Evidence that current or proposed action does not adequately resolve that risk.
prohibited_inferences: Do not import submarine go-deep doctrine into surface navigation.
Do not infer which vessel must act under COLREGs.
Do not prescribe a heading or speed, or predict a collision from the accident outcome.

chunk.report_title: MAIBInvReport 13/2020 - Stena Superfast VII and Royal Navy Submarine - Marine Incident
chunk.text: 18 An annex to COMOPS’s letter summarised the RN’s analytical findings, stating that: ● CPA occurred at 1256 at a range of 250 – 500yds. ● Stena Superfast VII detected the submarine’s periscope at range 800 – 1000yds – ordering a course alteration 20 seconds later. ● The submarine classified (visually) the Stena Superfast VII as Ferry at range 9 – 10kyds The annex also included diagrams showing the relative tracks of both vessels. In a second annex to COMOPS’s letter, the Commander of the Faslane Flotilla (COMFASFLOT) remarked that ‘it is already clear from post-event analysis that the submarine over-ranged the STENA Ferry, resulting in flawed decision making by the Submarine Command Team’. This annex also explained the actions taken by the RN as a result of the incident [Section 4]. On 9 April 2019, the Chief Inspector of Marine Accidents made a written request for a meeting between RN and MAIB staff to further review the case. This resulted in a meeting between MAIB inspectors and senior RN staff in Faslane on 1 July 2019, where further details of the event were disclosed and analysed in co-operation. 1.9 PREVIOUS SIMILAR ACCIDENTS 1.9.1 MAIB Report 20/20168: Collision between Karen and a dived Royal Navy submarine On 15 April 2015, an RN submarine was on passage and deep in the Irish Sea when it snagged the fishing vessel Karen’s trawl wires. Karen was dragged astern at about 7kts and partially submerged before the trawl wires parted under tension and it was released. The MAIB’s investigation established that the collision occurred because the submarine’s command team assessed that Karen was a merchant vessel, resulting in significant overestimations of the fishing vessel’s range and speed. The submarine was at a safe depth, therefore the command team did not perceive any risk of collision or need for avoiding action. The submarine’s command team had assessed that the majority of shipping contacts in the area were merchant vessels, when they were, in fact, mostly trawlers. This presented a significant hazard to the fishing vessels and the submarine and it was not safe for the submarine to try and proceed through the Irish Sea below periscope depth. There were sufficient clues on board the submarine to have identified the possibility of collision. Also, about 3 hours later, when the commanding officer became aware of the collision, the matter went unreported. 8 https://www.gov.uk/maib-reports/collision-between-the-stern-trawler-karen-and-a-dived-royal-navy- submarine

extraction.source_assessment: The passage combines administrative chronology with an explicit RN causal finding about range overestimation and MAIB findings from the Karen accident about misclassification, erroneous motion estimates, and unrecognised fishing-gear collision risk. These mechanisms support conditional lessons; the recorded manoeuvre timing and CPA do not establish recommended actions or thresholds. The reporting omission is not developed into a causal lesson for navigation decisions.

warning_signs: A decision relies on a range estimate that is contradicted by other available observations or has material unresolved uncertainty.
card.investigator_finding: Post-event RN analysis explicitly linked overestimation of the ferry's range to flawed command-team decisions.
card.transferable_lesson: Where range estimates are uncertain or inconsistent, assess the reliability of the range supporting a navigation decision rather than treating apparent distance as established safety margin.
non_transfer_conditions: No range-error mechanism should be asserted merely because a contact is closing or has a low CPA.
The passage supplies no general range-error magnitude, action threshold, or recommended manoeuvre.

supporting_quotes.quote: it is already clear from post-event analysis that the submarine over-ranged the STENA Ferry, resulting in flawed decision making by the Submarine Command Team

lessons.potential_decision_use: Flag a proposal whose safety justification depends on an inadequately supported range estimate and identify the need to resolve that uncertainty.
required_live_evidence: The provenance and uncertainty of the contact range, or explicit discrepancies between range observations.
Evidence that the current assessment or proposal depends materially on that range.
prohibited_inferences: Do not infer that a live range is overestimated from this accident.
Do not infer visual or submarine sensing methods, visibility, encounter geometry, or COLREG roles.
Do not reproduce the accident's course alteration or use its outcome to predict a live outcome.

warning_signs: Contact range or speed estimates depend on an unverified vessel-type classification.
Available observations conflict with the assumed contact type.
card.investigator_finding: The Karen investigation found that classifying a fishing vessel as a merchant vessel caused significant overestimation of its range and speed and contributed to the collision.
card.transferable_lesson: Treat vessel identity and motion estimates as linked uncertainties when the estimation process depends on assumed contact type. Reconsider the dependent estimates when classification is doubtful.
non_transfer_conditions: A vessel-type label alone does not establish that range or speed estimates depend on it.
Submarine-specific classification or sensing procedures are not transferable surface-vessel recommendations.

supporting_quotes.quote: The MAIB’s investigation established that the collision occurred because the submarine’s command team assessed that Karen was a merchant vessel, resulting in significant overestimations of the fishing vessel’s range and speed.
There were sufficient clues on board the submarine to have identified the possibility of collision.

lessons.potential_decision_use: Challenge confidence in a risk assessment when its range and speed inputs inherit uncertainty from an unverified classification; seek corroboration before relying on those inputs.
required_live_evidence: An uncertain or contradicted contact classification.
Explicit evidence that the range or speed estimation process uses that classification.
The observations available to corroborate or challenge the classification and estimates.
prohibited_inferences: Do not assume a live contact is a fishing vessel or is misclassified.
Do not assume an identity error corrupts independently measured range or speed.
Do not infer that unspecified clues from the accident are present in the live state.
Do not derive COLREG roles from the accident's contact labels.

warning_signs: An area-wide traffic assessment treats most contacts as one vessel category despite evidence of another category.
A proposed transit depends on that assumed traffic composition being correct.
card.investigator_finding: The submarine team incorrectly assessed most local contacts as merchant vessels rather than trawlers. Investigators identified the resulting traffic environment as hazardous and the attempted submerged transit as unsafe.
card.transferable_lesson: A shared mistaken assumption about multiple contacts can invalidate an area-wide navigation assessment. Check the evidence for traffic composition rather than extending one assumed classification across the traffic picture.
non_transfer_conditions: Multiple contacts alone do not establish a common classification error.
The finding that this submarine transit was unsafe does not establish a general prohibition on surface navigation among trawlers.

supporting_quotes.quote: The submarine’s command team had assessed that the majority of shipping contacts in the area were merchant vessels, when they were, in fact, mostly trawlers.
This presented a significant hazard to the fishing vessels and the submarine and it was not safe for the submarine to try and proceed through the Irish Sea below periscope depth.

lessons.potential_decision_use: Prompt reassessment of a transit proposal when its overall traffic model relies on common, weakly supported contact classifications.
required_live_evidence: Multiple contacts and the basis for their classifications.
Evidence of a shared classification assumption or conflicting observations.
An explanation of how the proposed transit depends on the assumed traffic composition.
prohibited_inferences: Do not infer that contacts are trawlers from their number or location alone.
Do not transfer submarine depth restrictions or doctrine to surface vessels.
Do not infer that every contact shares an error demonstrated for only one contact.

warning_signs: A safety assessment considers separation from a vessel but omits relevant deployed fishing gear.
An asserted safe operating condition is being treated as excluding all contact hazards.
card.investigator_finding: The submarine snagged Karen's trawl wires. Its team perceived no collision risk or need for avoidance because the submarine was at what was considered a safe depth.
card.transferable_lesson: A safety margin against a vessel itself does not necessarily address hazards from its deployed gear. Where gear presence and exposure are established, include that hazard rather than relying solely on the condition considered safe for hull separation.
non_transfer_conditions: This is a transfer of the omitted-hazard mechanism, not a submarine-depth recommendation.
The passage provides no fishing-gear clearance distance or universally safe CPA.

supporting_quotes.quote: On 15 April 2015, an RN submarine was on passage and deep in the Irish Sea when it snagged the fishing vessel Karen’s trawl wires.
The submarine was at a safe depth, therefore the command team did not perceive any risk of collision or need for avoiding action.

lessons.potential_decision_use: Identify an incomplete clearance assessment when a proposal addresses the vessel track but not explicitly evidenced fishing-gear exposure.
required_live_evidence: Evidence that fishing gear is deployed or may occupy the intended transit area.
Information sufficient to establish possible interaction between own ship and that gear, including uncertainty about its extent.
Evidence that the current safety justification omits this exposure.
prohibited_inferences: Do not infer deployed gear from a fishing-vessel label alone.
Do not infer gear position, dimensions, depth, or entanglement risk without live support.
Do not assume a hull CPA alone establishes either safety or danger from gear.
Do not prescribe submarine procedures, headings, or speeds.

chunk.report_title: MAIB Report 14/2021 - Achieve/Talis - Very Serious Marine Casualty
chunk.text: 6 Achieve’s skipper had been a fisherman for more than 40 years and had owned Achieve for 11 years. The deckhand had worked with the skipper on board the boat for four years. Both the skipper and the deckhand had completed all UK statutory safety courses4. In addition, the deckhand held a non- mandatory under 16.5m skipper’s certificate5. Position data A bulk carrier anchored off Tynemouth, 1nm away from the accident position, was fitted with a voyage data recorder (VDR)6, and MAIB recovered its data for analysis. Radar information was recorded and used to determine Talis and Achieve’s positions before the collision. MAIB plotted the positions (Figure 6) to determine the vessels’ aspect and Achieve’s relative movement, as seen from Talis, prior to the collision. Figure 6: Plot of Achieveʼs positions relative to Talis, recreated from third party VDR Date Range Rings Ship's course Ship's speed 8 November 2020 3nm 0.5nm 132° 8.2kts Relative track of Achieve Achieve true course 229°, speed 5.5kts Closing speed 10.8kts 1529 1533 Estimated range of first radar sighting 1540 0 0.5 270 260 250 240 230 220 210 200 190 180 170 160 150 140 130 120 110 100 90 80 70 60 50 40 30 20 100350 340 330 320 310 300 280 290 1 1.5 2 2.5 1541 HEAD UP 4 Anyone starting work on a UK registered commercial fishing vessel must complete one-day basic safety training courses for sea survival, firefighting and prevention, first aid, and health and safety. Experienced fishermen (those with two years’ experience) also need to complete a further one-day course in safety awareness and risk assessment. 5 MCA approved Seafish Skipper’s Certificate for Under 16.5m Vessels up to 20 miles off-shore. 6 Talis was not required to carry a VDR. It is required to be fitted to vessels 3000 gross tonnage and upwards.

extraction.source_assessment: Page 5 supplies crew experience and qualifications, describes recovery and use of third-party VDR radar data to reconstruct vessel positions, and presents a relative-track figure with motion data. It contains no investigator finding, causal conclusion, or explicit safety issue. The statement that MAIB plotted positions to determine aspect and relative movement describes analytical method, not a finding about navigation decisions. Neither the crew particulars nor the plotted encounter data alone supports a transferable lesson.
